intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees, the causative mutation is expected to be an extremely rare heterozygous variant, shared by all affected family members.
checks.explanation: The paper shows that heterozygous GNAL mutations cause PTD. It never uses the designation 'dystonia-25/DYT25'.

checks.claim: The GNAL gene is located on chromosome 18p11.
checks.evidence_quote: GNAL is located on chromosome 18p centromeric to the DYT7 locus
checks.explanation: The paper gives 18p. The 18p11 band is standard locus nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. Onset is usually in adulthood and most often in the neck (cervical dystonia). The dystonia may stay focal or spread to segmental or generalized forms, often involving cranial and speech muscles. Brachial onset has not been reported (Fuchs et al., 2013).

checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees
checks.explanation: The disease is a primary torsion dystonia with AD inheritance.

checks.claim: Onset of dystonia-25 is usually in adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: Average age of dystonia onset in the carriers was 31.3, and ranged from 7–54 years.
checks.explanation: The mean onset age points to adulthood, but the paper never says onset is 'usually in adulthood', and some patients had childhood onset.

checks.evidence_quote: Most carriers (82%) had onset in the neck

checks.evidence_quote: Brachial onset was not observed

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported 28 mutation carriers with definite dystonia from 8 families. Seven families were of mixed European Caucasian ancestry and 1 was of mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite ancestry. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82% of carriers, and 93% had neck involvement at their last examination. However, only 46% still had focal dystonia. Cranial involvement was seen in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. No patient had brachial onset, and only 32% developed arm involvement. The authors noted that this pattern distinguished GNAL dystonia from DYT6.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) gave details for each family. In family D1, onset in the 6 relatives of the proband ranged from 19 to 50 years. Each had segmental dystonia beginning in the neck, and in 1 relative each the larynx and trunk, or the face, were also involved at onset. The proband, a man, had onset in the legs at age 7 years and developed generalized dystonia. In the Mennonite family P, onset ranged from 25 to 48 years. Five members had neck onset, with focal, segmental, or generalized dystonia. The female proband had leg onset at 25 years and developed generalized dystonia. In family D2, the proband had jaw onset at 39 years. Two relatives had neck onset at 33 and 18 years, and a fourth relative had focal tongue dystonia beginning at 11 years. In family T, 2 men had focal neck dystonia beginning at 25 and 42 years, and a woman had segmental dystonia with laryngeal onset at 25 years. The other families (S, H, B, and N) consisted of patients with focal or segmental dystonia with neck onset, with ages at onset between 17 and 54 years.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) used exome sequencing in 2 families with primary torsion dystonia and identified heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene. Family P carried a nonsense mutation (S293X) and family D1 carried a missense mutation (V137M). Each mutation segregated with the disease in its family. Sanger sequencing of 39 additional multiplex primary torsion dystonia families that were negative for DYT1 and DYT6 found GNAL mutations in 6 more families (19%). These included a missense mutation (E155K), a nonsense mutation (R21X), 2 frameshift insertions, an in-frame 9-bp deletion, and a possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C). None of the variants were present in dbSNP135, in about 3,500 European exomes, or in 572 control chromosomes.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) studied the mutants with a BRET assay of Galpha-olf coupling to the D1 dopamine receptor. The S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses. The authors suggested that these results pointed to loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) used exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.409G-A transition in the GNAL gene in family D1, a mixed European Caucasian family with primary torsion dystonia. The mutation results in a val137-to-met (V137M) substitution. It was among 20 missense variants shared by all 4 exome-sequenced members and segregated with the disease in the family, which had 7 affected members. The male proband had leg onset at age 7 years and developed generalized dystonia. The other 6 affected members had segmental dystonia with onset between 19 and 50 years, beginning in the neck. In a BRET assay of D1 dopamine receptor coupling, the V137M mutant showed an intermediate phenotype that was largely consistent with impaired association with G-beta-gamma subunits.
